title: Central bankers eye higher rates as AI boom fuels scramble for cash
key_facts: Reuters, 16 Oct: central bankers at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok say the AI boom is setting off a global race for money and may keep interest rates higher.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh called it a shock that hits the demand side of the economy before the supply side, and warned the transition could be very bumpy.
ECB policymaker Martins Kazaks: investment in AI is one of the key factors driving up the cost of money.

South African Reserve Bank Governor Lesetja Kganyago said the neutral interest rate (R-star) is higher but nobody knows how high; Bank of England chief economist Huw Pill said rates may on average be a little higher.

The Bank of Japan has cited AI-related demand as a factor in its recent rate increases; economists expect the Bank of England to raise rates on 5 Nov; the ECB and Fed raised rates in September and markets price another move by both in December.
Sovereign bond yields have risen worldwide, some to levels not seen since before the global financial crisis; debt-laden France is seen as particularly exposed.
ECB President Christine Lagarde said France's first solution lies at home in fiscal policy.
quote_evidence: "If you're a central banker...you've got to recognise this as a shock," Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok.
"There is a global fight for money," ECB policymaker Martins Kazaks told Reuters.
"Maybe rates, on average, will be that little bit higher," said Bank of England Chief Economist Huw Pill.
why_it_matters_hint: If AI investment keeps pulling in money, borrowing may stay more expensive for governments, companies and households.
